section_summary: This section records communist-linked labor unrest in Japan in 1949, including the Taira police station incident, railway layoffs, and reactions to the death of railway president Sadanori Shimoyama. It also contains a report on a communist-sponsored peace meeting in Kamakura and a long historical study of Prince Fumimaro Konoe’s 1945 warning about a possible communist revolution.

subfiles.title: Text of General MacArthur’s Fourth of July Statement
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper clipping; enclosure to despatch no. 431
subfiles.about: MacArthur contrasts American democracy with communism and praises Japanese resistance to communist propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The clipping prints MacArthur’s statement describing communism as coercive and expressing confidence in Japan’s democratic development.

subfiles.title: Communist-led disorders at Taira
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports communist-led confrontations with police and the Fukushima Prefectural Assembly.
subfiles.summary: A crowd seized the Taira police station after a dispute over a bulletin board, while another demonstration forced the prefectural assembly to adjourn. Yoshida warned that labor unrest threatened recovery and foreign investment.

subfiles.title: The Communist Danger in Japan
subfiles.from: Cloyde K. Huston, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Assesses communist-linked railway labor unrest and the political effects of Shimoyama’s death.
subfiles.summary: The despatch connects growing disorder to railway layoffs and communist influence in the railway union. It discusses speculation about Shimoyama’s death, possible emergency measures, and the challenge of restoring order without alienating Japanese workers.

subfiles.title: The Communist Danger
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper editorial; enclosure to despatch no. 451
subfiles.about: Urges public opposition to what the editorial portrays as communist infiltration and intimidation.
subfiles.summary: The editorial calls for citizens and leaders to defend democratic institutions amid labor disturbances.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement notice for despatch no. 451
subfiles.about: Designates an attached copy of despatch no. 451 as the record copy.
subfiles.summary: The original action copy had not been returned.

subfiles.title: The Communist Danger in Japan
subfiles.doc_type: duplicate control copy of despatch no. 451
subfiles.from: Cloyde K. Huston, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Repeats the assessment of railway unrest, Shimoyama’s death, and possible responses to communist activity.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the despatch on railway layoffs, localized disturbances, speculation about Shimoyama’s death, and the difficulty of responding to violence while protecting public rights.

subfiles.title: Communist “Peace” Meeting in Kamakura
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards Zurhellen’s report on a communist-sponsored Kamakura peace meeting.
subfiles.summary: Sebald identifies the meeting as part of a Communist Party propaganda campaign.

subfiles.title: The Kamakura Peace Meeting
subfiles.from: J. Owen Zurhellen, Jr., American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Describes a Kamakura peace meeting and Sanzo Nosaka’s speech.
subfiles.summary: Zurhellen reports the meeting’s attendance, banners, speakers, and Nosaka’s arguments about war, independence, and foreign troops. He also recounts a brief exchange with Nosaka about freedom of speech.

subfiles.title: The Konoe Memorial of February 14, 1945
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards Spinks’s historical analysis of Konoe’s warning about communist revolution.
subfiles.summary: Sebald introduces the memorial’s publication and describes Spinks’s argument that Japanese leftists and rightist militarists shared an interest in state control and economic reform. He notes that the study’s conclusions are partly inferential.

subfiles.title: The Konoe Memorial of February 14, 1945
subfiles.doc_type: historical memorandum; enclosure to despatch no. 602
subfiles.from: Charles N. Spinks, Foreign Service Officer
subfiles.about: Examines the historical basis for Konoe’s fear that prolonging the war could enable communist revolution in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Spinks discusses the memorial’s provenance and argues that Japanese communists and radical rightists found common ground in anti-capitalist reform and Soviet-style planning. He traces research groups and personal advisory circles linked to Konoe, the Cabinet Planning Board incident, and the Sorge espionage case. The memorandum also reviews wartime Soviet-Japanese relations and concludes that informal advisers and research organizations offered channels for communist influence. Spinks presents several conclusions as tentative inferences.
